questions.stem: A patient takes levothyroxine with coffee and a calcium chew, and the thyroid-stimulating hormone keeps climbing. What is the best first step?

options.text: Fix the timing before changing the dose

questions.explanation: B is correct: the coffee and calcium were blocking absorption, so fix the timing before changing the dose. A treats the wrong problem. C treats an overactive thyroid. D is unsafe.

questions.stem: How should levothyroxine be taken? Select all that apply.

options.text: Or at bedtime, at least 3 hours after the last meal
About 4 hours apart from calcium, iron, and antacids
With morning coffee to help absorption
On an empty stomach with water

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and E are correct as taught. D is wrong because coffee grabs the drug in the gut and lowers absorption.

questions.stem: What is the full replacement dose of levothyroxine for a healthy younger adult?
questions.explanation: A is correct: about 1.6 micrograms per kilogram per day. B and D are tenfold errors. C is a low starting dose for older or cardiac patients, not full replacement.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with heart disease starts levothyroxine. How should it be started?

options.text: Full dose of 1.6 mcg/kg per day
Start low at 12.5 to 25 mcg and climb slowly

questions.explanation: B is correct: for older adults or anyone with heart disease, start low at 12.5 to 25 micrograms and climb slowly. A risks heart problems. C is for an overactive thyroid. D is wrong because doses are rechecked.

questions.stem: The levothyroxine dose was raised today. When should the level be rechecked?
questions.explanation: D is correct: the drug takes 6 to 8 weeks to settle. A and B give misleading results and invite the wrong dose change. C waits too long.

questions.stem: Which effects can too much levothyroxine cause? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: B, C, and D are correct: too much causes a fast heart, abnormal rhythms, and bone loss. E and A fit too little thyroid hormone, not too much.

questions.stem: Which antithyroid drug is the first choice for most patients with an overactive thyroid?
questions.explanation: C is correct: methimazole is the first choice for most patients. A is saved for special cases because of its liver warning. B treats an underactive thyroid. D is not taught as an antithyroid drug.

questions.stem: A patient on methimazole develops a sore throat with fever. What should happen?

options.text: Stop the drug and check a white count now
Take a throat lozenge and continue

questions.explanation: A is correct: both antithyroid drugs can rarely wipe out white blood cells. B and C ignore a possible emergency. D treats an underactive thyroid.

questions.stem: Which statements about thyroid drugs in pregnancy are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Raise levothyroxine as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Recheck about every 4 weeks through the first half of pregnancy
Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester
Methimazole can cause birth defects early in pregnancy

questions.explanation: A, B, D, and E are correct as taught. C is wrong because levothyroxine needs go up in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A patient on methimazole for Graves' disease is planning pregnancy in a few months. What is the best recommendation?
questions.explanation: D is correct: current guidance says to switch before conception so the first trimester is covered. A risks uncontrolled disease. B raises birth defect risk. C does not treat an overactive thyroid.
